## Abstract:

For large language models (LLMs) to guarantee the trustworthiness and consistency of data, hallucination detection is essential. According to current research, the LLM model can generate false and inaccurate data that compromises the models’ dependability. A review on hallucination detection in LLMs was given in this paper. This study distinguished between internal and external methods for detecting hallucinations. While external models rely on external tools, internal approaches rely on signals within the model. In addition to outlining future research possibilities, this work describes methodological categories, frameworks, applications, and distinctions between various hallucination detection approaches. This article offers organized knowledge about reliable LLM model developments and hallucination detection.

### I. Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) are currently tested in different text, image, and data processing applications, such as text summarization, sentiment analysis, virtual assistants, and content creation. Healthcare, banking, law, and education are just a few of the fields that use LLM models extensively \1\], \[2\], \[3\], \[4\]. However, there were serious problems with LLM models, such as factual reliability or hallucinations, large computational costs, and problems with reasoning and ethics. When an LLM experiences hallucinations, it generates material that looks authoritative and well-written, but it contains false information, contradicting assertions, factual errors, or unreliable information. Current surveys don’t make a basic distinction between detection strategies that operate inside the LLM’s architecture and those that need outside documents and knowledge sources to be verified \[5\], \[6\], \[7\], \[8\]. Internal model-based and external knowledge-based techniques are the two primary categories into which this research has separated hallucination detection methodologies in order to address these problems. This study examined methods that examine model confidence scores, attention patterns, hidden state representations, uncertainty measurements, and consistency over several generations for internal model-based approaches. This article investigated fact-checking against knowledge bases, retrieval-augmented verification, cross-referencing with reliable sources, and human-in-the-loop validation systems on the external knowledge-based side. Below is a list of this survey paper’s noteworthy contributions:
•

In order to automatically recognize hallucinations in writings generated by LLM, this work presents a single taxonomy that blends model-based and external knowledge-based approaches.

•

This survey study offers a thorough overview of automated detection techniques in both categories, combining various approaches like fact-checking, retrieval-augmented verification, model confidence analysis, and hidden state representations.

•

This work highlights important issues and potential avenues for future research while analyzing current standards and datasets.
